d.title: The wrong fix, which reads as reasonable API work
d.caption: **`get_orders(user_id: str)` is not identity, it is a parameter** — and a parameter is something the model fills in, from a conversation an attacker may be participating in. Any user, account or tenant id in a signature that decides whose data comes back makes your access control a prompt-injection target. **It is the most common serious mistake in MCP server design**, precisely because it looks like ordinary API design, and the server feels finished.

d.title: A one-method protocol, and the two fields that carry identity
d.caption: **`subject` is who the token was issued for and `claims` is an arbitrary dictionary** — tenant, roles, email — which is where identity actually lives. Note the distinction `client_id` draws: it identifies the *application*, so a bearer token shared by one client authenticates that client and not a person. **`required_scopes` is enforced before a tool runs**, so a token lacking the scope never reaches your code, and returning `None` from the verifier is the rejection.

state: who the token was issued for

d.title: Identity from context, never from the signature
d.caption: **`get_access_token()` takes no arguments** — it reads the verified token from the current request's context, the way a web framework exposes the current user. Note what the tool signature does not have: no `user_id`, so the model cannot influence whose orders come back because it is never asked. **And `limit` is still a parameter, correctly.** The test for whether something belongs in the signature is whether a hostile value would be a security problem or merely a strange request.

d.title: Identity is decoration unless it reaches the predicate
d.caption: **A tool that reads `token.subject` and then queries with an admin credential has established who is calling and asked for the data anyway.** The middle layer is correct and depends on every query being written correctly forever; the bottom layer is what survives a mistake — and the difference matters because a server accretes tools, and the twentieth will be written by someone who has not read this lesson. **The audience check in the top layer is the one people omit**, and it is what stops a token minted for another service being replayed at yours.

d.title: Over stdio there is nothing to put identity in
d.caption: **All of the above needs an HTTP transport, because the token arrives in a header.** Over stdio the server runs as whoever launched it, with their credentials, and that *is* the identity — which is usually fine, because a stdio server has exactly one user. **The mistake is not a single identity; it is a single identity serving per-user data.** A server exposing the same data to everyone is a perfectly good design: say so in the instructions, keep the tools read-only, and nobody has to audit it for identity handling.

d.title: Forty times faster, and that ratio is the whole argument
d.caption: **A suite that finishes in tens of milliseconds runs on every save; one taking a second per file runs before a release** — by which time the mistake has been built on. Almost all of the subprocess cost is interpreter startup, paid per test file at best and per test at worst. **The helper takes `mcp._mcp_server`**, the low-level object FastMCP wraps, which is the same private attribute lesson 1.2 used for the version and carries the same caveat.

d.caption: **Call the function directly for its logic — that needs none of this machinery.** What needs a client is the part MCP generated, and that is where the regressions are. **The third row is the highest-value line in the file:** converting `Annotated[str, Field(description=...)]` back to `str` is a plausible tidy-up by someone who has not measured what a docstring contributes, and it changes no behaviour while removing the documentation from every consumer's prompt.

d.title: Asserting listChanged is False, on purpose
d.caption: **The assertion reads oddly and that is the design: it is not that False is correct forever, it is that changing it should be deliberate.** Declaring `listChanged` without sending notifications leaves a caching client holding a stale list for the whole connection, with nothing erroring — lesson 1.2's warning, in executable form. The test fails the day someone turns the flag on, and somebody has to confirm the notifications exist before they can make it pass.

d.title: A fingerprint, and when it is worth the friction
d.caption: **It fails on any change to a name, a description, a schema or an output schema — including the ones you meant — and the failure message says what to do.** The point is that a change to your consumers' prompt cannot happen without somebody noticing. The executed version produced `43f8831a3a1bb42a`, stable across two calls. **For an internal server it will fail on every intentional edit and be updated without thought**, which is worse than not having it.

d.caption: **The fixture exercises the protocol honestly and deliberately skips the transport**, so the whole stdout class is invisible to it — a `print()`, a library logging to stdout, an import-time warning. **The division that works:** everything about the protocol and the schemas in process, where it is cheap enough to run constantly, plus exactly one deliberate smoke test over stdio for about a second, because that is the only thing that catches a real process's problems.

d.title: Nine surfaces, and the one that fails without an error
d.caption: **Every breaking row produces a failure somebody can see — inside a model's tool call, as a validation error nobody is watching for.** The description row is different: it changes the text in your consumers' model context, so their agent starts choosing your tool more or less often, and nothing anywhere reports it. **That is the rug-pull mechanism from the author's side**, and the reason a description edit deserves a changelog entry.

d.title: Versioning something the API cannot version
d.caption: **Lesson 1.2 measured the awkward part: `FastMCP` has no `version` parameter**, so by default every server reports the SDK's number and consumers cannot tell your releases apart. Set it through the private attribute anyway — it is the one field a consumer can alert on without hashing your tool list. **And semantic versioning here means the interface, not the implementation**, because that is what your consumers depend on; a number with no published meaning cannot be pinned against.

d.title: Four steps, and step three is the whole procedure
d.caption: **A deprecation window measured in dates is a guess; one measured in log lines is a fact.** If the warning is still firing, somebody's agent still depends on the tool and removing it will break them whatever the announcement said — and you cannot see your consumers, because there is no dependency graph and the caller may be an agent built once and left running. **Note where the notice goes:** the description is the only channel that reaches the model choosing the tool, so a clear notice reduces the calls rather than merely labelling them.

items.label: Add the replacement
items.desc: A new tool affects nobody, so this step is free and can ship immediately.

items.label: Mark the old one, and log it
items.desc: DEPRECATED with a removal date, delegating to the new one -- and a log line on every call.

items.label: Wait for the log lines to stop
items.desc: The only evidence that nobody depends on it. A server with no call logs cannot do this at all.

items.label: Remove it, bump the major
items.desc: Now safe, because you have evidence rather than an announcement.

d.title: Five fields, and the one that decides a deprecation
d.caption: **Their side sees a model's decision; yours sees what was actually called with what** — which is why only your logs can answer a consumer's question. **Note the outcome field doing double duty:** “which tools fail” and “which tools are used at all”, and the second is what tells you a tool can be removed. And log named fields rather than the whole argument dictionary, chosen per tool — harmless on a currency tool, personal data on a customer lookup, in a log you may keep for ninety days.

d.title: Five limits, and the one that needs identity
d.caption: **A published server has a new failure mode: a consumer whose agent loops.** Lesson 2.3 showed a model will retry an identical call when the error does not say `retryable: false`, and a looping agent can call your tool hundreds of times a minute. **The rate limit needs the caller identity from lesson 4.2 to be per-caller** — without it the only available limit is global, which converts one consumer's bug into everyone's outage and leaves you unable to say whose.

a huge result is resent on every later turn
your tool is somebody's blocked turn
over HTTP all callers share one process
the cheapest loop prevention there is

d.title: Two managers, and the argument that replaces rather than merges
d.caption: **The nesting is not stylistic: a session cannot outlive the transport carrying it.** `ClientSession` is transport-agnostic, so everything written against it works over streamable HTTP unchanged. **And the `env` row is a real afternoon lost:** a dictionary replaces the environment entirely, so the child loses `PATH`, `HOME` and on Windows `SYSTEMROOT` — and the symptom is a server that works when you run it by hand and fails under your client, which sends people looking in the server.

state: no PATH, no HOME, no SYSTEMROOT

d.title: The session group is the host-side fan-out, written once
d.caption: **Lesson 1.1 assigned this job to the host: one client per server, and somebody has to merge the lists.** `ClientSessionGroup` is that, with `group.tools` as the merged dictionary and `group.call_tool` routing by name — measured as three tools across two servers and two sessions held. **The reason it is the default for a service is the exit stack:** every subprocess is owned in one place, so there is no path that leaves a child running.

nodes.label: One exit stack owns every subprocess

d.title: It raises rather than shadowing - and the hook is the fix
d.caption: **Failing loudly is the right choice**, because the alternative is one server silently shadowing another's tool and nobody finding out. **Set the hook from the start rather than when a collision forces it**, because prefixing earns its place three times: collisions, legible traces that say where a call went, and the cross-server shadowing defence from lesson 4.1 — a description claiming to be about `transfer` is visibly not about `payments_transfer`. Keep the prefix short, since the model reads it.

d.title: A client in a handler leaks a process per request
d.caption: **The latency is the visible half — about 1.1 seconds of interpreter start before any work happens — and the leak is the half that pages someone.** A client owns a subprocess, so a handler that opens one leaks whenever teardown is skipped: a cancelled request, a timeout, an exception on an unusual path. **The symptom is memory exhaustion hours later with nothing in the agent logs**, which is why it survives testing. The fix is the same shape as a database pool.

d.title: Eight decisions, and three of them are the security module
d.caption: **Rows one, two and four are the controls from lesson 4.1, and all three live in client code.** That is the asymmetry worth ending on: a server author can write careful descriptions and hold a narrow credential, and none of it protects the consumer — because the consumer decides what to connect and what to expose. **Which is encouraging rather than alarming**, since the list is short and it is all code you own.

d.caption: **That is the real advantage of this surface: the allow-list and the prefix are in code, in version control, and visible in a pull request** where a reviewer can ask why a name is on the list. The same list buried in a configuration nobody reviews gives identical technical protection and far less assurance anyone considered it. **And note the last row:** `get_tools` is a live call at construction time, so a server that is down takes your agent with it and a slow one delays your startup.

d.title: The same server is a different risk in each column
d.caption: **A server with twenty tools, four of them destructive, behind a four-name allow-list is a reasonable thing to deploy; the same server in a desktop configuration exposes all twenty.** That is not an argument against desktop hosts — it is an argument for choosing servers differently depending on where they go. **For a laptop, prefer a server whose whole tool list you are comfortable with** and narrow its reach through its arguments; for a service, the allow-list lets you take a broader server and expose a slice.

d.title: The review question, in every column
d.caption: **Assuming the model does the worst thing available to it, what happens?** It survives the thing that defeats reading descriptions — the descriptions changing. **Note the second branch:** the worst tool that matters is the worst *reachable* one, which in a desktop configuration is every tool the server has rather than the ones you intended to use. The one-line version: connect the server you would be willing to leave connected while someone tries to talk your agent into misusing it.

d.title: One design decision, five modules of consequence
d.caption: **The protocol itself is small: a handshake, three primitives, three transports and an error shape.** Everything that took five modules follows from one fact — a server's text enters a model's context, and a server's tools act with the server's own credentials. **So you are trusting someone else's prose inside your prompt and someone else's access behind your tool calls**, and every control in the course is an answer to one half of that sentence.
